stem: After transplantation, when should bone mineral density be reassessed per standard bone-health references?

options.text: At six months post-transplant and then every 12 or 24 months thereafter
Only once at ten years post-transplant with no earlier reassessment
Never after baseline because immunosuppression prevents bone loss
Daily DEXA scans for the first year only

explanation.rationale_correct: DEXA screening includes baseline pretransplantation, reassessment at six months post-transplant, and every 12 or 24 months thereafter to assess bone health.

rationale_incorrect.B: Six-month and periodic reassessment is recommended rather than a single decennial study.
rationale_incorrect.C: Recipients remain at bone-loss risk and require ongoing DEXA monitoring.
rationale_incorrect.D: Periodic 12- to 24-month intervals are referenced rather than daily scanning.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 6, Noninfectious Diseases → Preserve bone health → Screen for decreased bone mineral density
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Six months posttransplant … Every 12 or 24 months thereafter to assess bone health

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 6 → Preserve bone health → DEXA at 6 months then every 12–24 months; PDF p. 322 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Post-transplant DEXA interval angle distinct from baseline pretransplant screening (cctc-2107) and osteopenia teaching (cctc-1047); anchor verified on Cupples p. 322.

stem: When teaching long-term skin surveillance, which anatomic distribution aligns with standard references for basal and squamous cell carcinoma in transplant recipients?

options.text: Seventy-five percent occur on the head, neck, or dorsal surface of the hands
All lesions occur exclusively on the soles of the feet
Lesions occur only on sun-protected mucosa with no head or neck involvement
Skin cancers never involve the hands or neck in transplant recipients

explanation.rationale_correct: Seventy-five percent of squamous and basal cell carcinomas in solid-organ transplant recipients occur on the head, neck, or dorsal surface of the hands.

rationale_incorrect.B: Head, neck, and dorsal hand surfaces are the predominant sites rather than soles alone.
rationale_incorrect.C: Head and neck are among the most common involved sites.
rationale_incorrect.D: The dorsal surface of the hands is a common site for these carcinomas.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 6, Noninfectious Diseases → skin cancer → Basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma
primary_anchor.quote_hint: 75% of squamous and basal cell carcinomas occur on the head, neck, or dorsal surface of the hands

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 6 → skin cancer → 75% of BCC/SCC on head, neck, or dorsal hands; PDF p. 280 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Anatomic distribution angle distinct from sun-exposed site teaching (cctc-3101) and 95% epidemiology (cctc-2105); anchor verified on Cupples p. 280.

stem: A coordinator compares cutaneous carcinoma behavior in transplant recipients with the general population. Which pattern aligns with standard references?

options.text: Skin lesions are more aggressive and multiple squamous cell carcinomas develop more frequently
Skin lesions are always benign and never recur after transplantation
Basal cell carcinomas never recur or metastasize in recipients
Transplant recipients develop fewer skin cancers than the general population

explanation.rationale_correct: Compared with the general population, transplant recipients have more aggressive skin lesions and develop multiple squamous cell carcinomas more frequently.

rationale_incorrect.B: Lesions are described as more aggressive rather than uniformly benign.
rationale_incorrect.C: Basal cell carcinomas in recipients are more likely to recur or metastasize than in the general population.
rationale_incorrect.D: Transplant recipients have markedly elevated skin-cancer risk rather than lower risk.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 6, Noninfectious Diseases → skin cancer → Evolution of cutaneous carcinomas
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Skin lesions are more aggressive … Multiple squamous cell carcinomas develop more frequently

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 6 → skin cancer → aggressive lesions and multiple SCC in recipients; PDF p. 280 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Aggressive lesion behavior angle distinct from anatomic distribution (cctc-3106) and SCC-versus-BCC frequency (cctc-2106); anchor verified on Cupples p. 280.

stem: A coordinator is updating long-term post-transplant health maintenance. Evaluate the following statements:

elements.text: Annual influenza vaccination is recommended unless otherwise contraindicated.
DEXA reassessment at six months post-transplant is part of bone-health monitoring.
Calcium and vitamin D supplements may be used to prevent or treat osteopenia or osteoporosis.
Bone mineral density never needs reassessment after the pretransplant baseline.

explanation.rationale_correct: Annual influenza vaccination, six-month DEXA reassessment, and calcium/vitamin D supplementation are recommended components of long-term care. Statement IV is false because DEXA is repeated at six months and every 12 or 24 months thereafter.

rationale_incorrect.A: Statement III is also true—calcium and vitamin D are listed for osteopenia/osteoporosis prevention or treatment.
rationale_incorrect.C: Statement I is also true; statement IV is false.
rationale_incorrect.D: Statement IV is false because ongoing DEXA monitoring is recommended after baseline.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 6, Noninfectious Diseases → Prevent infection / Preserve bone health
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Annual influenza vaccination … Six months posttransplant … Calcium and vitamin D supplements

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 6 → Prevent infection (annual influenza vaccine) and Preserve bone health (DEXA intervals, calcium/vitamin D); PDF p. 322 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Post-transplant infection-and-bone-health combo distinct from dental-care combo (cctc-3104) and skin-cancer combo (cctc-1105); anchor verified on Cupples p. 322.
